To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
Islamic specificity is not a major issue for Islamic banks in the region, and that the performance of Islamic and conventional banks is not different in the region.
Islamic banks in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region face specific risks related mainly to the PLS contracts and to some extent to other contracts.
Sharia compliance exerts a positive impact upon the performance of Islamic bank and specific risk has a negative impact on the performance of Islamic Banks.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the measurement of performance of Islamic banks, and the impact of specific risks upon their performance, and the extent to which specific risks are hedged by loan loss provisions.
the measurement and analysis of the performance of IBs in the MENA.
the measurement of the performance of Islamic Banks and the impact of specific risks upon their performance.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
specific risks do not matter.
the performance of Islamic Banks is not significantly affected by Sharia compliance or specific risks.
specific risks are a minor attribute for IB performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the performance of IBs in MENA region is not driven by Sharia specific contracts but rather by conventional contracts.
Islamic banks face specific risk related to Sharia compliant contract but the specific risk is not a major attribute of the performance of IBs.
the performance of Islamic banking is similar to the performance of conventional banking, and that Islamic banking is not more risky than conventional banking.
The main takeaway from our work is that
specific risks do not affect the performance of IBs in the MENA.
Islamic banks are more resilient to the 2007 2008 financial crisis than their conventional peers.
the performance of IBs is not driven by the specific nature of Islamic contracts.
